transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-09-10 16:00 UTC | Duration: 58m
Attendees: Liam Patel (Redwood AE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (CTO - Starlight), Aaron Kim (VP Eng), Sophie Laurent (ML Engineer), Devon Brooks (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick qualification on p95 targets, expected concurrency patterns, streaming requirements, and security/VPC constraints. Wants a pilot with Dedicated capacity if cost/latency alignment looks good.

Topics: p95 latency targets, steady-state concurrency, token/sec bursts, streaming/cancelation behavior, VPC/private deployment, audit logs/KMS, pilot scope and timelines.

Transcript:
00:00 Liam Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we got about an hour on the calendar, i'm liam from redwood, i'm the account lead, and with me is sofia our se.
00:06 Priya Malhotra: hey thanks liam, appreciate you carving out time, we have a tight window to decide on an inference strategy by end of quarter.
00:12 Aaron Kim: yeah hey all, i'll jump in with timelines — we have a pilot board review next week, so speed matters.
00:17 Sofia Alvarez: great, quick agenda — understand your production p95 targets, token throughput expectations, streaming vs batch patterns, and any security requirements that would push you to dedicated or private deployment.
00:28 Devon Brooks: and network, yep, we need to know VPC wiring, peering, and kms flow.
00:34 Sophie Laurent: plus the quality constraints — we can't degrade beyond a 3% regression on our NPS metric when switching quantized variants.
00:44 Liam Patel: good signal — let's start with latency SLOs. what are you targeting at p95 for your customer-facing chat and for async summaries?
00:53 Priya Malhotra: chat — we want p95 sub-300ms for short, 64-token responses. For longer contexts, 512 tokens, p95 of under 900ms ideally.
01:05 Aaron Kim: add to that concurrency — we expect 600 concurrent chat sessions during peak, average request size ~110 tokens, and bursts to 1,800 concurrent for short 16-token quick replies during flash sales.
01:20 Sofia Alvarez: okay that's useful. are those values for perceived latency end-to-end including client and network, or strictly inference server time?
01:26 Priya Malhotra: server-side, we measure from request reach to model byte stream — client-side adds another 50-80ms usually.
01:33 Liam Patel: perfect. that means our routing/batching behavior matters a lot. a couple quick questions: do you need streaming partial token outputs, and do you cancel mid-response frequently?
01:44 Sophie Laurent: yes streaming is central — users expect tokens as they generate; cancelation is moderate, maybe 8-10% of calls cancel mid-stream.
01:54 Devon Brooks: we also want deterministic fallbacks — if a hosted node is overloaded, the system should fail to a slightly cheaper/but-compatible model without dropping sessions.
02:03 Sofia Alvarez: we support automated fallback policies; we can route to a lower-cost quantized variant or a different region with warmed kv cache. quick note, some product names in our transcripts get munged, like KV cash.
02:15 Aaron Kim: (laughs) yeah, happens. okay on the p95 numbers, are you open to Dedicated capacity? sounds like 1,800 burst concurrency will need looked at differently.
02:23 Priya Malhotra: we're evaluating three options: Hosted (fast onboarding), Dedicated (reserved GPUs), or Private (VPC/on-prem). Ideally host for dev and Dedicated for pilot/production. Private only if compliance forces it.
02:34 Liam Patel: that's a common pattern. rough cost/latency trade-off: hosted gives fastest rollout but shared tenancy may create p95 variability during noisy neighbor events; Dedicated reduces variability and gives better predictable p95 at a higher baseline cost.
02:48 Sophie Laurent: what about autoscaling? our traffic is fairly spiky. we can't wait 5 minutes to scale up.
02:55 Sofia Alvarez: we have burst capacity options for Dedicated that let you pre-warm and instant-burst to reserved GPUs, and warm standbys for short-lived surges. also continuous batching reduces per-token cost without adding perceivable latency in steady state.
03:09 Devon Brooks: does continuous batching penalize streaming latencies? we're sensitive at the start of the stream.
03:15 Sofia Alvarez: good question — we can set conservative batching windows for streaming to prioritize first-token latency. then we ramp up batching for tail tokens or long contexts. that helps meet sub-300ms p95 for short replies.
03:30 Priya Malhotra: what about model variants? Sophie mentioned quantized variants — we need guidelines on when quality degradation is acceptable for cost savings.
03:38 Liam Patel: we recommend model A (float16) as baseline for quality. quantized variants (like 4-bit) for background tasks or lower-criticality flows. Redwood Optimize can run small evals on your prompt set and show expected quality delta. we can tie regressions to automated rollback rules too.
03:55 Aaron Kim: can you give an example token/sec and GPU sizing for our stated workload — 600 steady concurrency at 110 tokens average, bursts to 1,800 for short 16-token replies?
04:06 Sofia Alvarez: rough calc: assume each stream consumes X ms per token on a given GPU profile; for a 90B-ish model in fp16 on an A100-class profile, you'd expect about 60-80 tokens/sec per stream if single-threaded; but with batching we can reach much higher aggregate tokens/sec. for 600 concurrent at 110 tokens, that's 66k tokens/sec sustained. bursts: 1,800 * 16 = 28.8k tokens/sec but focused on very low latency — so we'd optimize for low queueing.
04:36 Priya Malhotra: those numbers feel... unexpected. can you put that into GPU counts?
04:40 Sofia Alvarez: sure — very rough: for fp16 with good batching, 1 GPU could handle ~15k-25k tokens/sec depending on kernel efficiency and sequence length distribution. so 66k sustained might map to 3-5 GPUs in a Dedicated pool with steady batching and prefix caching. bursts to maintain sub-300ms for short replies might require pre-warmed burst capacity — maybe an extra 4-6 GPUs on standby.
05:04 Devon Brooks: standby GPUs — cost model? we can't afford idle GPUs all day.
05:09 Liam Patel: reserved capacity is priced with a base commit and a burst pool that bills only when used (or a smaller warm standby fee). we can model your 95th percentile usage and optimize commit vs burst to minimize cost. we'll include a cost scenario in the follow-up.
05:22 Aaron Kim: service side, what telemetry do you expose? we need token-level latency, per-model p95, trace spans.
05:29 Sofia Alvarez: console provides token-level cost and latency breakdown, per-route dashboards, flame graphs for hot paths, and request tracing that shows queuing, kernel time, and network egress. logs are exportable to your splunk/etl.
05:42 Priya Malhotra: security — SOC 2 and KMS integration. our legal keeps asking about audit logs and customer-managed keys.
05:50 Liam Patel: we support SOC 2 attestation, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. for Private/VPC we can hand off a customer-managed KMS flow and we also provide detailed audit logs per request. i'll attach the big security packet after this call.
06:03 Devon Brooks: what about data residency? some of our users must remain in eu-west.
06:08 Sofia Alvarez: you can pin models to region; we support routing policies by region and automatic regional fallback. for strict residency we recommend Private deployment inside your VPC in the eu region or a dedicated region in our private offering.
06:20 Sophie Laurent: i'm curious about cancelation and memory — if a request is canceled mid-token does the GPU free memory instantly? we've had outages with lingering kv cache growth.
06:30 Sofia Alvarez: cancellations free in-flight compute quickly; we scrub the KV cache when sessions end after a short timeout. long-lived sessions can hold kv cache but we offer proactive eviction policies and cache sharding to prevent head-of-line issues.
06:43 Aaron Kim: lovely. ok, let's talk about an actual benchmark. we want Redwood to run a short p95/burst test using our sample prompts. what telemetry will you deliver?
06:52 Liam Patel: we'll run three scenarios: steady-state 600 concurrency at your 110-token average, burst 1,800 concurrency for 16-token replies, and streaming with 8-10% cancelation. metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (inference-only), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and per-request trace logs. we'll also try a fallback-to-quantized variant and measure quality delta.
07:10 Priya Malhotra: timeline?
07:12 Liam Patel: we can turn around a hosted-run within 48 hours if you provide prompts and auth; a Dedicated on-prem benchmark requires infra setup and may take 5-7 business days.
07:21 Sophie Laurent: can we run one prompt that is highly latency-sensitive and another that's long-history to measure kv cache benefit?
07:27 Sofia Alvarez: absolutely. send a small deck with the two canonical prompt types and we'll map them to test scripts.
07:33 Devon Brooks: will you need any network access from our side? we prefer to keep secrets internal.
07:38 Liam Patel: for hosted benchmarking, you'll provide sanitized prompts and a small credential token; for Dedicated pilot we can work with your security team to set up VPC peering or a private peering endpoint; secrets can be kept in your KMS for private deployments.
07:51 Aaron Kim: one more thing — what are SLAs on latency? we need contractual p95 SLOs.
07:57 Sofia Alvarez: Dedicated contracts can include latency SLOs in the agreement for specific routes/models; hosted has best-effort but we publish performance profiles and 99th/95th expected ranges. for enterprise we can include remediation credits tied to missed SLOs.
08:12 Priya Malhotra: okay, obstructions — our legal will definitely push for indemnity on data leaks; we need clarity on where sensitive PII touches model logs.
08:22 Liam Patel: we support redaction pipelines and can opt-out of log retention per route. for Private deployments you fully control log retention. we'll include these options in the security packet.
08:33 Aaron Kim: competitors — any gotchas you've seen with Anthropic or other vendors?
08:37 Sofia Alvarez: some vendors struggle with streaming granularity and autoscaling during rapid token bursts — either they over-batch and inflate first-token latency or underutilize GPUs. Redwood's continuous batching + warm burst model addresses that tradeoff.
08:51 Sophie Laurent: (muttering) we've seen vendor X flatten token throughput badly — hope redwood avoids that.
08:57 Liam Patel: we'll show a token/sec trace so you can verify we don't collapse throughput.
09:02 Priya Malhotra: let's cover pilot success criteria. what does success look like for your team?
09:07 Aaron Kim: for infra, success is consistent p95 < 350ms for short replies and <900ms for long-context, and ability to handle burst to 1,800 without >150ms queueing.
09:17 Sophie Laurent: for ml quality, success is <3% drop in our evaluation metric when using any optimized variant.
09:23 Priya Malhotra: for operations, success is seamless observability into token-level traces and the ability to run canary rollouts by route.
09:30 Liam Patel: great, we'll draft a pilot plan that maps those success criteria to acceptance tests.
09:34 Devon Brooks: action items for us — we'll need to provide sample prompts, network contact, and legal placeholders.
09:41 Liam Patel: and on our side we'll deliver cost scenarios, security packet, and a hosted benchmark within 48 hours.
09:49 Sophie Laurent: could we get a quick sketch of expected Dedicated commit vs burst pricing? even a ballpark figure helps the pilot board.
09:56 Liam Patel: yes we'll include three scenarios: conservative commit (higher base, lower burst cost), mixed commit with small warm standby, and minimal commit with higher burst usage.
10:06 Priya Malhotra: ok timeline recap?
10:09 Liam Patel: you send prompts + legal contact today, we'll run hosted benchmark in 48 hours and deliver results + cost scenarios. schedule a 1-hr bench review next tuesday to go over traces. if benchmarks align we sign a short pilot for Dedicated capacity.
10:21 Aaron Kim: sounds good.
10:24 Priya Malhotra: thanks everyone. real quick question — is there a minimum pilot size for Dedicated?
10:29 Sofia Alvarez: we typically start pilots at a 3-6 GPU commit depending on model size, but we'll size specifically for your workload to meet p95 goals.
10:36 Liam Patel: perfect wrap. i'll follow-up with calendar invites and the security packet. thanks all.
10:41 Devon Brooks: thanks.
10:42 Meeting end.

Notes (auto): there is some transcription noise (names and acronyms occasionally mis-typed), action items and next steps agreed. Starlight leans Hosted for quick benchmark then Dedicated pilot if cost/latency line up.
